title: Prefix caching technical deep dive - Omnify Solutions
summary: Redwood SE team reviewed a recommended prefix/prompt caching strategy for Omnify's multi-tenant workload. Discussion covered cache key design, safe eviction, hit-rate expectations, interactions with batching and quantization, and security concerns for VPC/on-prem deployments. Next steps: Redwood to share design doc, run a small benchmark pilot, and provide security artifacts for procurement.

header:
Date: 2025-08-12
Start: 14:00 PDT
Duration: 52 minutes
Location: Zoom
Recording: yes
Attendees: Laura Chen (Redwood AE), Rafael Ortiz (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (Redwood Product), Priya Kapoor (Omnify CTO), Markus Li (Omnify Infra Lead), Sana Ahmed (Omnify ML Eng), Connor Dale (Omnify Security)
transcript:
[00:00] Laura Chen: hey everyone thanks for hopping on. can you all hear me ok?
[00:03] Priya Kapoor: yes loud and clear, thanks.
[00:06] Rafael Ortiz: cool, we'll jump straight into the prefix caching deep dive — want to align on goals first, right? Latency SLAs and cost targets.
[00:15] Markus Li: for us latency 99p under 250ms for common flows, and we want at least a 30% reduction in per-token cost on high-volume prompts.
[00:24] Maya Patel: and also multi-tenant safety — Omnify runs many customer prompts in same model, so cache leakage is a big concern.
[00:31] Rafael Ortiz: absolutely. so quick agenda: cache keys and hashing, hit rate modeling, eviction policy, batching interactions, quantization effects on cache, and VPC/on-prem considerations.
[00:40] Sana Ahmed: sounds good. can we start with cache key scheme? we saw some weird behavior with naive prefix keys.
[00:47] Rafael Ortiz: sure. naive key is simply full prefix text; that's simple but brittle — small punctuation changes or templated variables blow up cardinality. recommended pattern is a tiered key: 1) normalized prompt skeleton (canonicalize whitespace, strip PII placeholders), 2) hashed context window (e.g., last N tokens hashed), 3) tenant id and model variant tag. the final key looks like tenant|model|skeleton_hash|context_hash.
[01:12] Priya Kapoor: skeletonization sounds good, how do you avoid over-normalizing and losing cold-start variance?
[01:18] Rafael Ortiz: good point. we keep two caches: skeleton-level cache for high reuse (short, static prefixes) and context-level cache for finer granularity. On a miss in context cache, we fall back to skeleton cache and potentially do partial KV hydration. that preserves quality.
[01:29] Markus Li: partial KV hydration? can you explain?
[01:32] Rafael Ortiz: yeah, so we persist intermediate KV snapshots for skeleton prefixes. when a new request arrives with extra context we merge the skeleton KV into the runtime and only compute the delta tokens. it avoids redoing the full prefix compute. there are tradeoffs for KV memory.
[01:45] Laura Chen: memory tradeoff is real — we need to size KV storage and define eviction policy carefully. Rafael, suggestions on eviction?
[01:52] Rafael Ortiz: LRU with weighted entries works well; weight by token-length and last-access frequency. also segregate tenant namespaces: each tenant gets reserved or burstable slots depending on plan. prevents noisy tenants from evicting others.
[02:04] Connor Dale: segregation is critical for us. politically we can't have another tenant's KV in our memory. is there hardware-enforced isolation?
[02:10] Rafael Ortiz: on Dedicated or Private deployments we can pin GPUs and provide strict tenant isolation; for hosted multi-tenant we do logical isolation and quotas. we never share raw prompt text across tenants in caches — keys are namespaced and encrypted at rest.
[02:22] Connor Dale: encrypted at rest is good — can you share KMS integration docs?
[02:25] Laura Chen: we'll include security artifacts in the follow-up.
[02:28] [03:00] Sana Ahmed: what's realistic hit rate? our signal shows a lot of templated prompts but with unique user data appended.
[03:06] Rafael Ortiz: depends on template reuse. for heavy templating we often see skeleton hit rates 40–60% and context-level hits 15–30%. combined effective token saving can be 20–45% depending on how much of the prefix is cacheable. We model hit rate as function of template entropy and tenant concurrency.
[03:22] Priya Kapoor: what about TTLs — do you recommend time-based expiry?
[03:26] Rafael Ortiz: mix of TTL and LRU. short TTL for prompts with user-specific dynamic fields (e.g., timestamps), longer TTL for stable system prompts. Also emit metrics so you can adjust.
[03:36] Markus Li: batching — we've seen batching improve throughput but increase tail latency. how does caching interact with batching?
[03:42] Rafael Ortiz: when you use prefix caches you reduce per-request compute, which can reduce batch formation delays — more requests become quick to serve. but you also need to ensure KVs are warmed before large batched requests to avoid stragglers. Redwood runtime supports asynchronous KV prefetch for anticipated sequences.
[03:56] Sana Ahmed: quantify the latency wins?
[03:58] Rafael Ortiz: in internal tests, when 40% of prefixes hit skeleton cache and 20% hit full context, median token latency dropped ~30% and 99p dropped ~20% on similar QPS, but numbers vary by model and sequence length.
[04:13] Maya Patel: quantization — does using int8 or q4_0 change cache behavior? e.g., are KVs compatible across quantization variants?
[04:19] Rafael Ortiz: good callout — KVs are model/variant specific. a KV produced by an int8 variant may not be directly usable on fp16 runtime because kernel numerics differ. we recommend tagging model variant version in the cache key. For quantized variants we also recommend more conservative fallback to re-compute when model pipeline changes.
[04:36] Priya Kapoor: so we need to align model pinning if we want to maximize cache reuse.
[04:39] Rafael Ortiz: yes — either pin the model variant for a rollout window or accept lower hit rates during variant transitions and warm caches proactively.
[04:46] [08:00] Markus Li: multi-tenant safety: how do you prevent leakage via shared embeddings or KV collisions?
[08:04] Rafael Ortiz: first, namespace keys per tenant; second, scrub and canonicalize prompts to remove PII before caching (or avoid caching prompts with PII entirely); third, don't expose cache read APIs cross-tenant. Also periodic audits: we can sample caches and assert namespace separation.
[08:18] Connor Dale: sampling caches — is that safe? we don't want logs with actual customer prompts.
[08:22] Rafael Ortiz: we can sample hashes only, and verify namespace separation without storing cleartext. we can also enable allowlist caching policies for customers that require stricter controls.
[08:31] Sana Ahmed: curious about cache warm-up strategy — do you precompute for top flows?
[08:34] Rafael Ortiz: yes, recommended: 1) profile traffic to identify top skeletons, 2) precompute KV for those during off-peak, 3) keep cold-start fallbacks to a smaller model or serve via a hot path. Redwood supports scheduled warm-up jobs in Dedicated and Private.
[08:46] Priya Kapoor: if we run on-prem, do we get the same tooling?
[08:49] Rafael Ortiz: Private deployments include the same runtime features; certain managed services like metrics ingestion may need connectors. key management integrates with customer KMS/HSM.
[08:58] [12:00] Laura Chen: ops questions — what's the memory sizing calculator look like?
[12:04] Rafael Ortiz: it's simple: expected number of skeleton entries * average KV size + eviction headroom. KV size is roughly proportional to prefix tokens * per-token KV vector size (model dependent). we'll share a sizing spreadsheet; rough rule: reserve 2x peak working set for safety.
[12:18] Markus Li: can we limit per-tenant memory?
[12:20] Rafael Ortiz: yes, per-tenant caps with burst buckets; non-critical tenants can be throttled to avoid noisy neighbor.
[12:26] Maya Patel: instrumentation — what metrics do you recommend?
[12:29] Rafael Ortiz: cache hits/misses per key tier, KV load latency, eviction rate, per-tenant mem usage, hit-rate by template, token-cost savings, and tail-latency with/without cache. Redwood can export these to Prometheus/Grafana.
[12:41] Priya Kapoor: potential pitfalls?
[12:44] Rafael Ortiz: over-aggressive caching of prompts with dynamic user context (leading to stale outputs), not versioning keys by model variant, and insufficient namespace isolation. Also watch for evictions causing correlated latency spikes.
[12:56] Sana Ahmed: curious about privacy regs — if we cache templates that include PHI by mistake, how reversible is purge?
[13:02] Rafael Ortiz: keys and values can be purged; we also support TTLs and tenant-scoped deletion calls. For Private, you control storage and retention policies. We'll show the purge APIs.
[13:12] [20:00] Laura Chen: let's walk through a small example from Omnify — Sana, can you describe a representative prompt?
[20:15] Sana Ahmed: sure, we have a customer-support template: "Summarize customer message and suggest next-step (customer_id=XYZ, message=...)" — the skeleton is the text "Summarize customer message and suggest next-step" and the variables are customer_id and message.
[20:30] Rafael Ortiz: perfect. skeleton cache will store KV for that template; when unique message arrives we merge and compute only the message encoding. should save substantial compute if many messages share the same skeleton.
[20:40] Markus Li: question: how large are typical KV blobs?
[20:43] Rafael Ortiz: depends on model size. for a 7B model KV per token might be ~1–2KB, for 70B it's larger. exact numbers in sizing spreadsheet.
[20:52] Priya Kapoor: what's the pilot plan? we want to validate hit rates and tail latency on our traffic.
[20:56] Rafael Ortiz: propose a 1-week hosted pilot on a sampled tenant subset: Redwood will deploy skeleton caching with namespace isolation, run benchmark script against your sample prompt corpus, collect metrics. We'll measure hit rates, per-token cost savings, and tail latency.
[21:10] Laura Chen: timeline — we can start pilot after we get prompt corpus and sign off on security docs.
[21:15] Priya Kapoor: ok. procurement asks for SOC2 and infra diagrams.
[21:18] Laura Chen: we'll send SOC2 report and network diagrams.
[21:21] [30:00] Markus Li: edge case — what if prefix contains user-provided code or instructions that could alter model state?
[30:05] Rafael Ortiz: we treat prompts with executable content as non-cacheable by default. You can opt-in but we'd recommend strict allowlist and monitoring.
[30:14] Sana Ahmed: any tooling for detecting PII automatically before caching?
[30:17] Rafael Ortiz: yes we include an optional PII detector pre-check; if PII is detected, the prompt is either scrubbed or skipped for caching based on policy.
[30:25] Connor Dale: encryption in transit and at rest?
[30:29] Rafael Ortiz: TLS in transit; at rest we encrypt cache and KVs with customer-managed KMS for Private, and for hosted we offer Redwood-managed KMS or customer KMS via IAM.
[30:38] Priya Kapoor: audit logs for cache access?
[30:41] Rafael Ortiz: yes, per-request tracing and audit logs available in Redwood Console; you can filter by tenant, key namespace, operations.
[30:50] [40:00] Maya Patel: performance knobs — any parameters to tune for our workload?
[40:04] Rafael Ortiz: key knobs: skeleton window length (how much of the prefix you treat as skeleton), KV compression (space/speed tradeoff), per-tenant memory cap, async prefetch concurrency, and model pinning windows. We can iterate during pilot.
[40:16] Laura Chen: any estimate on cost savings?
[40:19] Rafael Ortiz: ballpark for heavy templated workloads: 20–45% token compute savings, which translates roughly to equivalent cost decreases depending on model price. We'll provide modeled estimates for your traffic once we see sample corpus.
[40:33] Priya Kapoor: are there any limitations with our VPC setup? we want traffic to stay inside our cloud account.
[40:38] Rafael Ortiz: for Private you can host everything inside your VPC. For Dedicated we can set up VPC peering and private network paths. Hosted will require egress to Redwood but we can use private links for secure connectivity depending on region.
[40:52] Connor Dale: procurement will want SLAs on cache durability and eviction behavior.
[40:56] Laura Chen: noted — we'll include implied durability and eviction docs in the materials.
[40:59] [47:00] Sana Ahmed: quick question — how do you measure effective token savings?
[47:05] Rafael Ortiz: we compute delta between tokens executed on model with and without cache for same workload. Also show cost-per-request before/after and normalized tail-latency. We'll send sample metrics dashboards.
[47:16] Priya Kapoor: last question — can we simulate cache misses at scale to see worst-case?
[47:20] Rafael Ortiz: yes, benchmark script includes cold-start and miss-heavy scenarios. We'll run both and report.
[47:27] Laura Chen: ok wrapping up — recap next steps: send design doc, security artifacts, pilot plan, and benchmark scripts. Omnify to provide prompts and compliance list.
[47:37] Priya Kapoor: thanks everyone this was super helpful.
[47:40] Rafael Ortiz: thanks, we'll follow up with materials.
[47:44] Laura Chen: thanks all, end call.
notes: Redwood will include cache key naming conventions and example pseudocode in design doc.
Pilot will be hosted first to collect metrics; Private deployment discussed as next phase.
Security: provide SOC2, network diagrams, and KMS integration notes.
